title: The proportions of different gases in the atmosphere

notes.definition: For about the last 200 million years the proportions of gases in the Earth's atmosphere have stayed much the same as they are today: about four-fifths (approximately 80%) nitrogen, about one-fifth (approximately 20%) oxygen, and small proportions of other gases.
explanation: The atmosphere is the layer of gases that surrounds the Earth. It is a mixture, not a compound, so the gases are not chemically joined and their proportions can be given as percentages by volume. AQA expects you to know the approximate figures: about four-fifths of the air is nitrogen (N₂) and about one-fifth is oxygen (O₂). More precise values for dry air are about 78% nitrogen and about 21% oxygen, but in the exam the rounded values of 80% and 20% are accepted.

The remaining small proportion is made up of various other gases. These include carbon dioxide (CO₂), water vapour (H₂O) and the noble gases (Group 0 elements), mainly argon. Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04% of the atmosphere, yet it is very important because plants use it for photosynthesis and it is a greenhouse gas. The amount of water vapour varies a lot from place to place and from day to day, so tables usually give the composition of dry air.

These proportions have been much the same for about 200 million years. Before that, the atmosphere changed greatly over billions of years: the early atmosphere had a lot of carbon dioxide and little or no oxygen. The atmosphere we have today is the result of those long-term changes, and it has been fairly stable on a geological time scale since then.

Many exam questions on this topic test data handling rather than recall. You may be asked to convert a fraction to a percentage (one-fifth = 20%), to work out the volume of a gas in a given volume of air (20% of 100 cm³ = 20 cm³ of oxygen), to read values from a pie chart or bar chart, or to change units, for example 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³. Always show the calculation and give the unit.

A useful way to check a percentage composition is that all the percentages must add up to 100%. If nitrogen is about 78% and oxygen is about 21%, then all the other gases together must be about 1%. This kind of reasoning helps you to fill in missing values in a table or pie chart.
keyFacts: The atmosphere is a mixture of gases.
Nitrogen makes up about four-fifths (approximately 80%) of the atmosphere.
Oxygen makes up about one-fifth (approximately 20%) of the atmosphere.
Small proportions of other gases are present, including carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases.
Argon is the most common noble gas in the air (just under 1%).
Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04% of the atmosphere.
The proportions of gases have been much the same for about the last 200 million years.
The percentages of all the gases in a sample of air add up to 100%.

keyTerms.definition: The layer of gases surrounding the Earth.
Two or more substances that are not chemically combined; air is a mixture of gases.
The unreactive elements in Group 0, such as argon, neon and helium; they make up a small proportion of the air.
The volume of one gas as a percentage of the total volume of the gas mixture.
Air with the water vapour removed; used for comparing compositions because water vapour content varies.

equations.name: Percentage of a gas in a sample
equations.formula: percentage of gas = (volume of gas ÷ total volume of sample) × 100

workedExamples.title: Volume of oxygen in a sample of air
workedExamples.question: Calculate the volume of oxygen in 2.5 dm³ of air. Use the approximate AQA value for the percentage of oxygen. Give your answer in cm³.
steps: Oxygen is about one-fifth of the air, which is 20%.
Convert the volume to cm³: 2.5 dm³ × 1000 = 2500 cm³.

workedExamples.title: Finding a missing percentage
workedExamples.question: A sample of dry air contains 78.1% nitrogen and 20.9% oxygen. Calculate the percentage of the other gases.
steps: All the percentages add up to 100%.

workedExamples.title: Working out a percentage from experimental results
workedExamples.question: A student passes 100 cm³ of air backwards and forwards over heated copper, which removes the oxygen. The volume of gas left at the end is 79 cm³ (example data). Calculate the percentage of oxygen in the air sample.
workedExamples.answer: 21%, which agrees with the accepted value of about one-fifth.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the air is mostly oxygen because we breathe it.
misconceptions.right: In fact about four-fifths of the air is nitrogen; oxygen is only about one-fifth.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think carbon dioxide is a major part of the air.
misconceptions.right: In fact carbon dioxide is only about 0.04% of the atmosphere, although it is important for photosynthesis and as a greenhouse gas.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the composition of the atmosphere has always been the same.
misconceptions.right: In fact it has been much the same only for about the last 200 million years; the early atmosphere was very different.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think air is a compound of nitrogen and oxygen.
misconceptions.right: In fact air is a mixture; the gases are not chemically bonded to each other and can be separated by physical methods.

realWorld: Divers' air cylinders and hospital oxygen supplies are prepared knowing that normal air is only about 20% oxygen.
Nitrogen, oxygen and argon are separated from air on an industrial scale and sold, for example argon for welding and filling light bulbs.
Weather stations measure the water vapour content of the air (humidity) separately because it changes from day to day.
examTips: Learn the AQA wording: about four-fifths nitrogen and about one-fifth oxygen. Writing 80% and 20% is fine.
When asked to name other gases in the air, give carbon dioxide, water vapour and a noble gas such as argon.
In calculations, check that your percentages add up to 100% and convert dm³ to cm³ (× 1000) before calculating if the answer is needed in cm³.
If a question gives a pie chart, measure or read the angles carefully: 360° represents 100%, so 1% is 3.6°.
summary: The atmosphere is a mixture of gases.
Small amounts of carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases make up the rest.
These proportions have been much the same for about 200 million years.
Percentages of all gases add up to 100%.

questions.question: Which gas makes up about four-fifths of the Earth's atmosphere today?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is about 80% of the air. Oxygen is only about 20%, and carbon dioxide and argon are present in small proportions.

questions.question: Approximately what percentage of the atmosphere is oxygen?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is about one-fifth of the atmosphere, which is 20%. 80% is the figure for nitrogen.

questions.question: Which statement about the air is correct?
options: Air is a compound of nitrogen and oxygen.
Air is a mixture of gases.
markScheme: 1 mark: air is a mixture of gases
questions.explanation: The gases in air are not chemically bonded together, so air is a mixture. It is mostly nitrogen, not carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Which group of gases is present in the atmosphere only in small proportions?
options: Nitrogen, carbon dioxide and water vapour
Oxygen, carbon dioxide and noble gases
Carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases
questions.explanation: AQA lists carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases as the small proportions of other gases. Nitrogen and oxygen are the two main gases.

questions.question: For about how long have the proportions of gases in the atmosphere been much the same as they are today?
questions.explanation: The atmosphere has been fairly stable for about 200 million years. 4.6 billion years is the age of the Earth, and the atmosphere changed a lot over that time.

questions.question: Which of these is a noble gas found in the atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Argon is in Group 0 and is the most abundant noble gas in air. Nitrogen is in Group 5, and methane and ozone are compounds or molecules that are not noble gases.

questions.question: A pie chart shows the composition of dry air. Which angle should represent oxygen if oxygen is 20% of the air?
questions.explanation: 360° represents 100%, so 1% is 3.6° and 20% is 20 × 3.6 = 72°. 288° would represent 80% (nitrogen).

questions.question: Why do scientists usually quote the composition of dry air rather than ordinary air?
options: The amount of water vapour in air varies.
Water vapour is not a gas.
Dry air contains more oxygen than ordinary air at all times.
markScheme: 1 mark: the amount of water vapour varies
questions.explanation: Water vapour changes with weather and location, so removing it lets compositions be compared fairly. Water vapour is a gas and does not react with nitrogen in the air.

questions.question: Which ratio of nitrogen to oxygen in the atmosphere is closest to the AQA figures?
questions.explanation: About four-fifths nitrogen and one-fifth oxygen gives 4 : 1. The ratio 1 : 4 is the wrong way round.

questions.question: A sample of dry air is 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen by volume. Which value is the best estimate of the percentage of carbon dioxide?
questions.explanation: The other gases make up about 1% in total, but most of this is argon (about 0.9%). Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04%.

questions.question: A student says: 'Because the proportions of gases have been the same for 200 million years, the amount of each gas in the air never changes.' Which is the best reply?
options: The student is right: no gas ever changes.
The student is wrong because oxygen has doubled in 200 years.
The proportions are roughly constant overall, but the amounts of some gases, such as water vapour and carbon dioxide, vary.
The student is wrong because nitrogen is now one-fifth of the air.
markScheme: 1 mark: proportions roughly constant but some gases vary
questions.explanation: The main proportions have been much the same, but small variations happen: water vapour varies with weather, and carbon dioxide levels change. Oxygen has not doubled and nitrogen is still about four-fifths.

questions.question: Calculate the volume of nitrogen in 500 cm³ of air. Use the value that nitrogen makes up 80% of the air.
Oxygen is about one-fifth of the atmosphere. Write one-fifth as a percentage.
Calculate the volume of oxygen in 2.0 dm³ of air. Use the value that oxygen makes up 20% of the air. Give your answer in cm³.
questions.explanation: Convert first: 2.0 × 1000 = 2000 cm³. Then 0.20 × 2000 = 400 cm³. Answering 0.4 forgets to convert to cm³.

questions.question:
Example data: a student passed 250 cm³ of air over heated copper to remove the oxygen. The final volume of gas was 198 cm³.
Calculate the percentage of oxygen in the air sample.
questions.explanation: The decrease in volume is the oxygen removed: 52 cm³. 52 ÷ 250 × 100 = 20.8%, close to the accepted one-fifth.

questions.question: A sample of dry air contains 78.08% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen and 0.93% argon. All the remaining gases are other trace gases. Calculate the percentage of the remaining gases.
questions.explanation: 78.08 + 20.95 + 0.93 = 99.96. 100 − 99.96 = 0.04%. This is roughly the percentage of carbon dioxide in the air.

questions.question:
Carbon dioxide makes up about 0.04% of the atmosphere. 1% is equal to 10 000 parts per million (ppm).
Convert 0.04% into parts per million.
questions.explanation: 0.04 × 10 000 = 400 ppm. Carbon dioxide levels are often reported in ppm because the percentage is so small.

questions.question: Name the two gases that make up most of the Earth's atmosphere.
questions.explanation: Nitrogen (about four-fifths) and oxygen (about one-fifth) together make up about 99% of dry air.

questions.question: Give the approximate fraction of the atmosphere that is nitrogen.
questions.explanation: AQA uses 'about four-fifths', which is approximately 80%.

questions.question: Name one noble gas that is present in the atmosphere.
markScheme: 1 mark: argon (accept neon, helium, krypton or xenon)
questions.explanation: The noble gases are Group 0. Argon is by far the most common in air.

questions.question: Name two gases, other than nitrogen, oxygen and noble gases, that are found in small proportions in the atmosphere.
questions.explanation: AQA lists carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases as the small proportions of other gases.

questions.question: Explain why air is described as a mixture rather than a compound.
markScheme: 1 mark: the gases are not chemically combined/bonded
1 mark: so they keep their own properties / can be separated by physical methods / proportions can vary
questions.explanation: In a compound elements are chemically bonded in fixed proportions. In air the gases are just mixed, so the composition can vary slightly and they can be separated, for example by fractional distillation of liquid air.

questions.question: Example data: a pie chart of dry air has a nitrogen sector of 281°. Calculate the percentage of nitrogen shown. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
questions.explanation: 360° represents 100%, so 281 ÷ 360 × 100 = 78.06%, which rounds to 78%.

questions.question: Water vapour is usually left out of tables of the composition of air. Suggest why, and explain how this affects the percentages of the other gases.
acceptedAnswers: percentages of other gases slightly lower in moist air
markScheme: 1 mark: the amount of water vapour varies (with location, temperature or weather)
1 mark: in moist air the percentages of the other gases are slightly lower because water vapour takes up part of the volume
questions.explanation: Because water vapour content is so variable, using dry air allows fair comparison. Adding water vapour makes the total include another gas, so every other percentage drops slightly.

questions.question:
Example data: Sample A of air has 20.9% oxygen and Sample B, taken in a crowded closed room, has 20.1% oxygen.
Calculate the percentage decrease in oxygen from Sample A to Sample B and suggest a reason for the difference.
markScheme: 1 mark: people in the room use oxygen in respiration (and release carbon dioxide)
questions.explanation: Percentage change uses the original value: 0.8 ÷ 20.9 × 100 = 3.83%. Breathing people use oxygen for respiration, which lowers the oxygen percentage slightly in a closed room.

questions.question: A student says the atmosphere is 80% nitrogen and 21% oxygen. Explain why these two values cannot both be exact.
markScheme: 1 mark: there are also other gases, so the values must be rounded/approximate (about 78% nitrogen)
questions.explanation: Percentages of all the gases must add up to 100%. The accurate values are about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, leaving about 1% for other gases. 80% is a rounded value.

questions.question: Describe the composition of the Earth's atmosphere today. Include approximate proportions and name the other gases present.
markScheme: Indicative content: atmosphere is a mixture; about four-fifths (80%) nitrogen; about one-fifth (20%) oxygen; small proportions of other gases; carbon dioxide (about 0.04%); water vapour (varies); noble gases such as argon (just under 1%); proportions much the same for about 200 million years.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): nitrogen and oxygen with correct approximate proportions, and at least two other gases named.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two correct points, for example 'mostly nitrogen'.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives both main gases with their proportions, names carbon dioxide, water vapour and a noble gas, and may mention that the composition has been stable for about 200 million years.

questions.question:
Example data: four samples of dry air were analysed.
Site 1: nitrogen 78.1%, oxygen 20.9%
Site 2: nitrogen 78.0%, oxygen 21.0%
Site 3: nitrogen 78.2%, oxygen 20.8%
Site 4: nitrogen 79.6%, oxygen 19.4%
Evaluate whether these data support the statement that the atmosphere is about four-fifths nitrogen and about one-fifth oxygen. Include calculations in your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content: four-fifths = 80% and one-fifth = 20%; sites 1 to 3 give nitrogen about 78% and oxygen about 21%, close to these values; mean nitrogen for sites 1 to 3 = 78.1%, mean oxygen = 20.9%; each pair adds to 99%, leaving about 1% for other gases (argon, carbon dioxide); site 4 is an anomaly: oxygen lower and nitrogen higher; possible reason: oxygen used up (for example combustion or respiration in a closed space) or experimental error; anomaly should be repeated or excluded; conclusion: data support the statement as 'about' four-fifths and one-fifth, but values are slightly less than 80% for nitrogen; more sites and repeats would increase confidence.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): calculations used correctly, anomaly identified with a reason, and a clear, justified conclusion about how well the data support the statement.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some comparison of data with 80% and 20%, with at least one calculation or the anomaly identified, and a conclusion.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example 'nitrogen is about 78% so it is about four-fifths'.
questions.explanation: To evaluate, compare data with the claim, process data (means), deal with the anomaly, and reach a justified conclusion. The word 'about' matters: 78% is close enough to four-fifths.
